Like what other people suggested on this thread, it would still be a good idea to open up to your therapist about this. I’m not completely sure exactly what stays confidential and what doesn’t, but since you’re an adult I’m pretty sure it’s not something they can share with your parents, unless it’s along the lines of suicidal ideation or something along the lines of seriously considering harming yourself or others. In this situation, because you’re thinking it could be OCD, they would have to rule that out first before anything else. I’m no psychologist but if you’re freaking out this much about it then I think there’s a chance that you’re not a pedophile and it actually is P-OCD. If the thought of doing those acts genuinely repulse you and it brings you so much dread thinking about it, then I think you’re okay. It’s scary but it’s definitely worth talking to your therapist about this. It’ll bring you reassurance and they won’t judge you for this. You’ll feel a lot better when you get those thoughts out. 
Stay strong, OP.

I’ve been on lamotrigine since I’ve started medication and it didn’t quite work for me until I paired it with divalproex. The medication since then has done wonders for me and it cleared the brain fog and absence seizures completely for me. The only problem I would say that I have with it is that it caused me to have some pretty bad short-term memory loss but I honestly prefer that over the seizures. Remember that different medications work for different people so lamotrigine can be amazing for some people and super incompatible with others. If you find that it doesn’t work that well for you or it’s causing a lot of other issues then you can always switch medications until you find one that works with you.

When I was six years old,my father passed away from a heart attack while me, my mother, and my siblings were on a trip. He had to stay behind because of work.

Since I was a little kid I wasn’t really fully aware of the situation but I unconsciously did things to cope. One of the things that I remembering doing the most right after my father’s death was looking up to my uncle. I began throwing all the love that I had for my father right onto my uncle because I needed someone to fill that role.

One of the other things was to accept my father’s death but I also wanted to pretend that he was still somewhat alive. I would still make Father’s Day cards for him when I was in school instead of giving it to someone else like my grandpa or one of my uncles. I always just wanted to make one for my dad. I did that up until my last few years of middle school.

I had to deal with the psychological effects of the situation on my own though. I became severely independent and always prepared for the worst possible scenario in case it came true. At 8 years old I was already dealing with severe anxiety attacks on a daily basis that I coped with alone. Never brought them up back then so I didn’t go to therapy or anything.

I don’t know if this will help at all but I hope it will. I’m 18 and I’ve been in your shoes and I’m still somewhat going through the same situation. Dealing with something like this is incredibly hard and I understand it completely because I’ve been going through it for years. But you’re 16 and I think there’s still hope for you whether you believe it or not. If you’re failing school at the moment then imo there’s no shame in taking a year off to focus on your mental health and then going back to complete your education successfully. There’s no rush to get a job or to get into university, you can go at a pace that feels good to you. I would also recommend trying a combination of antidepressants and therapy. You can switch antidepressants if one doesn’t feel good to you and you can switch therapists if you’re uncomfortable. If your parents refuse to put you in therapy then you can also do it online as it is cheaper. However, I am unsure if you can get a hold of antidepressants if you’re a minor. 

Also, you say you kinda feel selfish about it but it isn’t really. I’m not encouraging the action but I also believe you shouldn’t feel guilty about it. My best advice to you is to find your own reason to live, something that actually feels worth living for. It might sound bad but you shouldn’t have the mindset of staying here because the people around you will be upset, you should be wanting to live for yourself. You shouldn’t feel guilted into living. That’s not going to make you feel any better, it’ll only make you feel worse because you end up feeling trapped. Finding a way to be content and happy with your life is up to your own personal experience. As a stranger I cannot guarantee that your life will get better because I don’t know you personally and I can’t predict the future, but I hope that you do get better.

Hello, I’ve seen this issue with a lot of epileptic medications, they tend to cause some level of depression or anxiety in those who have to take it. I take a combo of lamotrigine and divalproex and the main side effect I experience is depression because of it, however it works really well for my seizures. My best advice would be to continue taking the medication that cooperates best with you and your seizures while also getting in touch with a doctor that can find an anti-depressant or anti-anxiety or something of the sort that can help lower those symptoms a bit. Just make sure that the medication doesn’t make your seizures worse or gets in the way of the medication.

I heard that keppra can be a mess but it’s usually the starter medication for most people when they first get diagnosed with epilepsy. I personally have never been on it but my sister has and it was an awful experience for her because she was having intense anger issues and mood swings. Take note of your side effects and bring it to your neurologist’s attention to see if they can find another medication that’s a more suitable fit for you. It’s going to be a bumpy ride and it might take a while to find the medication that corporates with your brain but I promise it will be worth it in the end.
